sec.title: Aims
sec.p: Residual cardiovascular risk remains substantial in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) despite high-intensity statin therapy. Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors (PCSK9i), including monoclonal antibodies and small-interfering RNA agents, offer additional risk reduction, yet comparative evidence across individual regimens remains limited.

sec.title: Methods and Results
sec.p: We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluating approved PCSK9i dosages in patients with ASCVD. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE); the secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularization, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause death. A total of eight trials involving 49,847 patients were included. Evolocumab (140 mg every 2 weeks or 420 mg monthly) and alirocumab 150 mg every 2 weeks significantly reduced MACE compared with placebo (risk ratios (RR): 0.78, 95% confidence intervals (CI): 0.66–0.93 and RR: 0.47, 95% CI 0.25–0.86, respectively). Evolocumab was also associated with reductions in myocardial infarction, stroke, and revascularization. Alirocumab 150 mg demonstrated the most pronounced effect on revascularization and was superior to both evolocumab and the lower alirocumab dose in this outcome. No regimen significantly reduced cardiovascular or all-cause mortality.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These findings suggest that PCSK9 inhibitors are effective in ASCVD, with generally similar efficacy across agents; however, regimens achieving lower and sustained low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels may confer greater benefit, in line with the concept that “the lower, the better.”

tr.td: PCSK9 inhibitors provide effective reduction of major cardiovascular events in patients with ASCVD, with broadly comparable efficacy across different agents.
Treatment strategies that achieve deeper and more sustained LDL-C lowering appear to yield greater clinical benefit, reinforcing the paradigm that “the lower, the better.”

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, despite the widespread implementation of evidence-based therapies such as high-intensity statins [1, 2]. In patients with established ASCVD, a substantial residual risk persists even after aggressive lipid lowering, highlighting the need for additional therapeutic strategies [3, 4]. This high-risk population typically presents with atherosclerotic plaques exhibiting characteristics of instability, which confer an elevated risk of adverse cardiovascular events [5].

In this context, the therapeutic modulation of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) has emerged as a biologically compelling and clinically impactful approach. PCSK9 inhibitors (PCSK9i)—monoclonal antibodies such as evolocumab and alirocumab, as well as small-interfering RNA agents such as inclisiran—have reshaped the landscape of lipid management by enabling profound and sustained reductions in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels [6]. Their clinical efficacy in reducing cardiovascular events has been demonstrated in multiple placebo-controlled trials conducted in patients with ASCVD [7–13]. However, differences in molecular mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, dosing intervals, and trial populations have raised questions about an existing “class effect” of these agents in reducing cardiovascular events.

In the absence of head-to-head comparisons, treatment selection is often guided by practical considerations—including adherence, dosing frequency, and tolerability—rather than expectations of differential efficacy [14, 15].

To address this gap, we conducted a comprehensive network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of different PCSK9i regimens in patients with established ASCVD, aiming to provide a structured and clinically informative overview of the available comparative evidence.

sec.title: Eligibility Criteria and Literature Search
sec.p: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) enrolling adult patients with established ASCVD who were treated with a PCSK9i (evolocumab, alirocumab, or inclisiran) at an approved dosage. Eligible trials were required to report at least one clinical cardiovascular outcome, including major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularization, cardiovascular death, or all-cause death. Trials enrolling primary prevention patients without evidence of ASCVD or individuals with ASCVD risk equivalents (e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia without prior events) were excluded. We also excluded nonrandomized studies, observational designs, and studies lacking outcome data. In all included trials, the comparator arms consisted of either placebo added to background statin therapy or standard statin therapy alone.

The literature searches and all analyses were conducted according to the Cochrane collaboration and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) statements. The study protocol is available in Supplementary Methods 1 and was registered in PROSPERO (ID: CRD420251022108).

sec.title: Definition of Clinical Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint was MACE, analyzed on a time-to-first-event basis. When MACE and its definition were explicitly reported in the original trial, we adopted the trial-defined composite. When MACE was not reported as a composite, we derived it by aggregating the individual endpoints that are conventionally part of three- or four-point MACE (i.e., cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and coronary revascularization) [16], as available from each study.
The secondary endpoints included all-cause mortality, as well as the individual components of the MACE composite—namely, myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, and revascularization.

sec.title: Data Extraction and Quality Assessment
sec.p: Two investigators (L.R. and F.M.S.) independently screened titles and abstracts of all records retrieved through the search strategy to assess potential eligibility, using Rayyan—a web-based platform developed to assist in the systematic review screening process [17]. The same two authors independently extracted data from eligible studies. A third investigator (V.G.) verified the consistency of data extraction and decided upon controversies. The final list of included studies was decided upon discussion between authors with full agreement required prior to inclusion.

Risk-of-bias assessment was conducted by two authors in duplicate (L.R. and F.M.S.) by using the version 2 of the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for RCTs (RoB 2), evaluating five domains of bias for each outcome: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, the measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported results (Supplementary Methods 2).

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: A Bayesian hierarchical network meta-analysis was performed using the BUGSnet package on R.

Fixed- and random-effect models were selected for each outcome on the basis of the smallest deviance information criteria. Analyses were performed using the Markov-chain Monte Carlo methods, based on 100,000 iterations with a burn-in of 10,000. Convergence was assessed with the Gelman–Rubin convergence diagnostic test. A frequentist random-effect network meta-analysis was also performed using the packages netmeta and dmetar on R. All outcomes were analyzed as risk ratios (RRs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Two-tailed P-values of 0.05 were used for statistical significance. The P-score statistic was used to assess the mean probability of superiority of each strategy to alternative treatments for a given outcome. Statistical heterogeneity was tested using the I2 values.

sec.title: Overview of Included Trials and Patient Characteristics
sec.p:
Our search identified eight eligible RCTs [7–13, 18] and included a total of 49,847 patients (Supplementary Fig. 1 PRISMA flowchart). Among the included trials, four evaluated evolocumab (n = 14,504), three assessed alirocumab—including 9,492 patients treated with 75 mg every 2 weeks (Q2W) and 148 with 150 mg Q2W—and one investigated inclisiran (n = 781). The mean follow-up ranged from 3 months to nearly 3 years. The baseline characteristics of the studies included are presented in Table 1. The characteristics of the network are shown in Fig. 1. sec.title: Primary Endpoint: Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events
sec.p: Among the included PCSK9i regimens, two demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in MACE compared with the placebo. Particularly, evolocumab 420 mg monthly (QM)/140 mg every 2 weeks (Q2W) showed a significant effect on the composite outcome (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.66–0.93). Similarly, Alirocumab 150 mg Q2W was associated with a significant reduction in MACE (RR: 0.47, 95% CI 0.25–0.86). Other regimens did not show statistically significant reductions in MACE compared with placebo (Fig. 1).

In comparisons between agents, a statistically significant difference was observed between alirocumab 150 mg and inclisiran, favoring alirocumab in terms of MACE reduction (RR: 0.37, 95% CI 0.16–0.83). No other indirect comparisons among PCSK9i showed statistically significant differences for the primary endpoint (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Secondary Endpoints: Myocardial Infarction, Stroke, Revascularization, and Mortality
sec.p:
Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality and the individual components of the MACE composite: myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, and coronary revascularization. Among these, evolocumab 420 mg QM/140 mg Q2W was associated with a statistically significant reduction in myocardial infarction, revascularization and stroke compared with placebo (RR: 0.72, 95% CI 0.56–0.90, RR: 0.77, 95% CI 0.67–0.88 and RR: 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.94, respectively). Alirocumab 75 mg Q2W significantly reduced the incidence of stroke (RR: 0.71, 95% CI 0.54–0.94), while alirocumab 150 mg Q2W demonstrated statistically significant effects on both stroke (RR: 0.13, 95% CI 0.01–0.93) and revascularization (RR: 0.39, 95% CI 0.20–0.74) (Table 2). Notably, in the case of revascularization, comparisons between agents showed that alirocumab 150 mg Q2W was associated with a statistically significant reduction in events compared both with alirocumab 75 mg Q2W (RR: 0.45, 95% CI 0.22–0.87) and with evolocumab 420 mg QM/140 mg Q2W (RR: 0.51, 95% CI 0.25–0.97) (Table 2).
None of the evaluated PCSK9i regimens were associated with a significant reduction in cardiovascular death or all-cause mortality compared with placebo (Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 2).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p:
In this network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials including patients with established ASCVD, we assessed the comparative efficacy of different PCSK9i regimens on major cardiovascular outcomes. Our results indicate that, while several strategies showed significant benefits on specific endpoints—such as myocardial infarction, stroke, or revascularization—only evolocumab 420 mg QM/140 mg Q2W and alirocumab 150 mg Q2W significantly reduced MACE versus placebo. No regimen demonstrated consistent superiority across all outcomes, and indirect comparisons did not show significant clinical differences, with the exception of a statistically significant advantage of alirocumab 150 mg over inclisiran and evolocumab 420 mg QW/140 mg Q2W in reducing MACE and revascularization; however, data on inclisiran are limited to a single trial including only 781 patients.Fig. 2

sec.title: Comparison with Previous Meta-analyses
sec.p: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first network meta-analysis to compare individual PCSK9i regimens and dosages in patients with established ASCVD, focusing on clinical cardiovascular outcomes.

Two recent network meta-analyses have explored the role of PCSK9i in cardiovascular prevention, though with markedly different aims and methodological frameworks compared with our study. Toth et al. [19] focused primarily on LDL-C lowering, comparing PCSK9i with other lipid-lowering agents such as ezetimibe and bempedoic acid. While valuable from a mechanistic standpoint, their analysis did not assess clinical cardiovascular outcomes, nor did it focus on a specific risk population. Wang et al. [16], by contrast, addressed clinical endpoints including all-cause mortality and myocardial infarction but included a mixed population of patients with ASCVD and ASCVD risk equivalents, introducing heterogeneity in the selection of the baseline population. Moreover, their analysis pooled different dosing regimens of the same agents and did not stratify results by individual PCSK9i dosage or schedule.

Our study differs in key aspects. First, we included only patients with established ASCVD, ensuring a clinically more homogeneous population where the pathophysiological substrate of plaque instability, inflammation, and thrombosis renders patients more responsive to intensive lipid-lowering strategies. Furthermore, we evaluated the individual PCSK9i regimens and dosages separately—except for evolocumab 140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM, which were analyzed together owing to their established clinical equivalence—providing a more nuanced understanding of their potential differential effects, including inclisiran, despite the currently limited evidence available for this agent.

sec.title: Mechanism of Action of PCSK9i: Beyond LDL-C-Lowering
sec.p: PCSK9 is a hepatic protease that plays a key role in lipid metabolism by promoting the degradation of LDL-C receptors on the surface of hepatocytes. By binding to LDL-C receptors, PCSK9 targets them for lysosomal degradation, thereby reducing their availability to clear circulating LDL-C cholesterol. PCSK9i are monoclonal antibodies or small interfering RNA that block this interaction or silence the translation of PCSK9 messenger RNA, respectively, enhancing the recycling of LDL-C receptors to the cell surface, and ultimately increasing hepatic clearance of LDL-C particles from the bloodstream [20]. This mechanism results in a profound and sustained reduction in plasma LDL-C levels, which is the primary driver of their cardiovascular benefit.

However, evidence suggests that the benefits of PCSK9i extend well beyond mere lipid modulation, particularly in patients with established ASCVD. In this population, atherosclerotic plaques are often characterized by a thin fibrous cap, large lipid core, and active inflammation, rendering them prone to rupture and thrombosis [5]. In addition to improving clinical outcomes when used to guide PCI [21–23], intravascular imaging has also demonstrated that PCSK9, when added to high-intensity statin therapy, induces favorable changes in coronary plaque composition; these include the thickening of the fibrous cap, reduction in lipid core, and decreased macrophage infiltration, indicative of plaque stabilization and reduced vulnerability [11, 12].

These structural modifications, observable within just 12 months of therapy, underscore a mechanistic rationale for the early and clinically significant reduction in MACE observed in trials. Moreover, when considered in the context of the PROSPECT study [5], these findings acquire further clinical significance, as many recurrent events have been shown to arise from angiographically mild but high-risk nonculprit plaques, which may be particularly responsive to intensive LDL-C lowering therapy.

sec.title: Clinical Implications
sec.p: In light of these mechanistic insights, the clinical implications of PCSK9i are most compelling in patients with established ASCVD, where vulnerable plaque morphology and residual inflammatory risk are prominent, although real-world data consistently demonstrate their underuse in eligible patients [24, 25]. A key methodological strength of the present network meta-analysis is the inclusion of patients with clinically manifest ASCVD, rather than a broader population that includes ASCVD risk equivalents, which often lack the advanced plaque phenotype—and thus the same potential for short-term benefit from PCSK9 inhibition—seen in patients with prior myocardial infarction, stroke, or revascularization. By focusing on a pathophysiologically coherent, high-risk population, this study enhances both the internal validity and clinical relevance of its findings. It allows for a clearer delineation of the comparative effectiveness of different PCSK9-targeting agents in a setting where their mechanistic potential can be fully expressed. Furthermore, this design aligns closely with contemporary clinical practice guidelines, which emphasize the prioritization of PCSK9i in patients with documented ASCVD and suboptimal LDL-C control despite maximally tolerated statin therapy. Taken together, our findings highlight a series of observations. While several PCSK9i regimens demonstrated statistically significant effects on individual MACE components—such as myocardial infarction reduction with evolocumab 420 mg QM/140 mg Q2W, stroke prevention with alirocumab 75 mg Q2W, and a broader endpoint improvement with alirocumab 150 mg Q2W—these results should be interpreted as exploratory signals rather than definitive evidence of superiority. The benefit observed with evolocumab 420 mg QM/140 mg Q2W on composite MACE is supported by robust evidence base and reinforces its role in ASCVD patients. A statistically significant indirect comparison between alirocumab 150 mg Q2W and inclisiran was observed for MACE, favoring alirocumab. However, this result should be interpreted with caution, as it is based on limited data—specifically, a single trial both for alirocumab 150 mg Q2W and for inclisiran—raising the possibility that the observed difference may reflect trial-level variability rather than a true difference in clinical efficacy. Notably, revascularization was the only secondary outcome showing significant differences in both direct and indirect comparisons, with alirocumab 150 mg Q2W emerging as the only regimen associated with a reduction in events compared with both evolocumab 420 mg QM/140 mg Q2W and alirocumab 75 mg Q2W. While these findings may suggest a greater impact of higher-intensity PCSK9 inhibition by alirocumab on ischemia-driven interventions, they remain exploratory and must be interpreted with caution: the apparent differences between evolocumab and alirocumab may reflect differences in trial design and populations—e.g., FOURIER enrolling patients with stable ASCVD and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES including post-acute coronary syndrome patients with a slightly longer follow-up—rather than intrinsic biological disparities between the two agents. Moreover, evidence from FOURIER and its open-label extension (FOURIER-OLE) [26] underscores that not only the magnitude but also the duration of LDL-C lowering is a key determinant of cardiovascular benefit, supporting the paradigm of “cholesterol-years exposure” as a driver of long-term outcomes and as an essential concept for interpreting the results of the present analysis. As such, these findings should be viewed as hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in adequately powered, direct head-to-head trials before guiding clinical decision-making.

sec.title: Study Limitations
sec.p: This analysis has several limitations that need to be mentioned. First, the network was constructed with strict inclusion criteria, which—while ensuring methodological rigor and enhancing the internal validity of comparisons, offering a more focused and clinically interpretable assessment of PCSK9i efficacy in patients with established ASCVD—also limited the number of eligible trials. Second, the definitions of MACE varied slightly across the included trials, with several reporting trial-specific composites and others requiring reconstruction from individual components, which may have introduced a degree of variability. Third, sample sizes were not uniformly large, and follow-up durations varied across studies, reducing the generalizability of the results. Additionally, evidence on inclisiran and alirocumab 150 mg Q2W was limited to a single trial, which may reduce the robustness of related estimates. Finally, safety outcomes were not systematically collected or analyzed in this network meta-analysis, reflecting the predominant focus on efficacy endpoints across the included trials. Nonetheless, the well-established safety profile of PCSK9i, as documented in the multiple large-scale randomized studies, partially mitigates the limitations associated with the absence of formal safety data in this analysis.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: PCSK9i represent an effective therapeutic option in patients with ASCVD. While certain PCSK9i regimens demonstrated statistically significant effects on specific cardiovascular outcomes, our findings suggest that the comparative efficacy among agents appears broadly similar, but they seem to favor high dosages to obtain lower and stable levels of LDL-C, in line with the famous sentence “the lower, the better.”
